doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Keeping Cannonball's talk on the record
summary: He explains why he kept Cannonball's stage talk at the start of the record as a gamble.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: I forgot to warn you but I think you learned on the job very quickly that when I get started the toughest thing is how do you interrupt and get to ask another question or change the subject. —his whole attitude and his sincerity and his warmth. He was a hell of a human being. And you know the thing was that I had been intrigued by his carrying on and talking to the audience at a time when what was much more normal was the Miles Davis turn your back, then leave the bandstand during the other guy’s solo kind of approach. And Cannon was this whole ongoing thing, and with talking to the audience, and not talking down but just talking. And it was something that we had it on tape and I just decided it was — sometimes some of the most successful things you do you look back and they represent, like weird gambles that you took. Because the whole idea, like here’s like at least a

twelve minute track but we’re a minute and twenty seconds into it before there’s a note of music, and that’s the beginning of the record. The beginning of the record is Cannonball introducing this song and talking about it, and then beginning to play it. And it’s the kind of thing, well if it had been a bad idea and it had led to the record flopping we wouldn’t necessarily have known it as a bad idea because it just wouldn’t have happened and nobody would have been particularly aware of it. So the nice thing about taking chances like that is if you lose the penalty is just obscurity and nobody keeps track of that, you’re kind of expected to be obscure most of the time with jazz records. But if it succeeds, what a wonderful idea, what a fabulous technique.
